canberra.title: Funding rows and route debates shadow the proposed Dunns Creek Road project
canberra.snippet: The planned Dunns Creek Road will serve as “an alternative strategic route” for motorists in southern NSW, but a route will n...
canberra.content:
Work on a cross-border route in southern Australia is ongoing – but not without controversy. Photo: Village Building Co.

The planned Dunns Creek Road will serve as “an alternative strategic route” for motorists in southern NSW, but a route will need to be locked in first.

Dunns Creek Road is set to connect Tralee (or South Jerrabomberra) in NSW with Canberra. There is currently one access road, which relies on Tompsitt Drive.

Queanbeyan-Palerang Regional Council (QPRC) is moving ahead with the project to avoid a ‘pinch point’ developing on that road.

An August 2026 information sheet from the council warns that problems could develop by 2031.

“In the long term, Dunns Creek Road will connect to an upgraded intersection at Isabella Drive,” the document outlines.

“We are working with the ACT Government to find an interim solution for the connection into the ACT as it will be some time before that intersection can be upgraded.”

The council’s plans to build a second cross-border route have been marred by controversy over which path to take.

In a recently released options report prepared by Stantec on behalf of the council, eight routes are considered, with several being examined in depth.

Of the latter options, one (labelled Option 5) was adopted as QPRC’s preferred alignment in 2015.

This route would be about 7.43 kilometres in length and cross Jerrabomberra Creek about 300 meters north of existing homes in Googong, before connecting into the Old Cooma Road and Googong Road intersection.

“Towards the eastern end of this alignment, Option 5 impacts on two Biodiversity Conservation Stewardship sites and the Wandiyali Wildlife Sanctuary before it connects into the Old Cooma Road and Googong Road intersection,” the report states.

“To minimise this, the existing road reserve between the two Stewardship sites can be utilised; however, this may result in a significant amount of cut being required.”

Another possible route, Option 2A, was assessed for both single- and double-lane configurations.

This option would connect to a proposed roundabout at Isabella Drive, before ultimately connecting to Old Cooma Road.

In response to questions from Region, Acting Minister for City and Government Services Chris Steel said he was committed to working with QPRC on a design.

But he said Canberra’s position remained that a cross-border link would need to use Isabella Drive.

“[This route] must include a new, safe and efficient intersection on the Monaro Highway at Isabella Drive, including a new grade-separated intersection, not just a connection to Tralee Street in Hume.

“This connection is only feasible if the NSW Government and the Commonwealth Government agree to jointly fund the project, including the intersection.

Ultimately, the Stantec report assessed the road as set to play a role as an “alternative strategic route”, and reduce traffic congestion on the Monaro Highway and Old Cooma Road.

“Overall, the Dunns Creek Road [DCR] corridor is shown to play a significant role in increasing broader network capacity in 2036 and 2041,” it outlined.

The routes were assessed against a design criteria that included a minimum speed of 70 km/h.

According to the report, construction is expected to kick off in 2033.

It also calls for a multi-stage approach to keep the price down, with estimates ranging from $5.97 million to $238.37 million depending on the option adopted by the council.

“This would benefit QPRC via a staged funding and delivery approach to minimise short term, large capital expenditure,” the report states of the staged approach.

Once this round of feedback concludes, QPRC councillors are set to receive a report later this year.

At that point, they’re set to vote on whether they’ll move ahead with the project (and the proposed route).

Village Building CEO Rob Fisher told Region that they would be watching the outcome of consultation closely.

“Village Building encourages increased access and provision of services across the ACT-NSW border,” he said.

“Dunns Creek Road enables better connectivity and improved commutes for residents on both sides of the border, and we are supportive of council’s engagement process. Sensible cross-border coordination is the key to the future of housing supply and employment land in the Capital Region.

“We look forward to working with NSW, the Commonwealth, and the ACT to progress this important infrastructure.”

You can give feedback on the options report through the Your Voice QPRC portal until 6 October.

canberra.title: Remorseless killers learn fate 27 years after taking Irma Palasics’ life
canberra.snippet: Two killers have finally been sentenced 27 years after causing the death of 72-year-old grandmother Irma Palasics in a brutal home invasi...
canberra.content:
Irma Palasics (middle) was killed by Joseph Vekony (left) and Steve Fabriczy (right). Photos: ACT Policing/Supplied.

Two killers have finally been sentenced 27 years after causing the death of 72-year-old grandmother Irma Palasics in a brutal home invasion that shocked Canberra and resulted in a decades-long mystery.

Steve Fabriczy and Joseph Vekony, both aged 71 and from Melbourne, were found guilty of manslaughter after a 39-day jury trial in the ACT Supreme Court. Both were acquitted of murder.

On Friday (28 August), Vekony was sentenced to 20 years’ jail with a 12-year non-parole period, while Fabriczy was handed 16-and-a-half years’ jail with 11 years non-parole.

Both sentences were backdated to the time of their arrests in 2023.

Justice David Mossop said unknown intruders first broke into the Palasics’ home in Red Hill in June 1997 and stole $102,000 cash.

Then on 10 October 1998, Vekony and another person broke into the Palasics’ garage and began searching the area before Irma interrupted them. Vekony repeatedly punched her in the face before fleeing, although she managed to pull off his balaclava before he did.

Justice Mossop said Vekony must have been aware of the success of the 1997 burglary, which provided a motive for the 1998 burglary as well as the home invasion the following year.

On 6 November 1999, Fabriczy and Vekony wore balaclavas and carried cable ties, duct tape and a metal bar when they broke into Irma’s home in McKellar before assaulting and tying up her and her husband, Gregor Palasics.

The intruders ransacked the home before stealing about $30,000 cash from a hidden compartment. They also drank from a water container and a milk bottle in the fridge, leaving their DNA behind.

Gregor eventually freed himself before he found Irma, dead, in the hallway, her airway full of blood.

Irma and Gregor Palasics, pictured when they lived in Red Hill. Photo: Supplied by family.

Justice Mossop said the intruders knew the Palasics were elderly before the break-in, as Vekony had assaulted Irma the year before.

He also said they ransacked almost every room in the house, which meant they would have had to walk around or over Irma’s body in the hallway.

“It is not reasonably possible that one of them was unaware she was bound and lying on the floor,” he said.

Justice Mossop said Irma had been left with extensive blunt force injuries, a broken nose and was covered in bruises and abrasions. Her cause of death was blunt force injury in some way, with an asphyxia component.

The judge did say he was unable to distinguish between the roles Vekony and Fabriczy played that night.

“The motive for the conduct was greed,” he said.

The DNA samples left on the drink containers in the Palasics’ fridge could not be identified for years.

But in 2008, Fabriczy and two others came up with a plan to hijack a Linfox truck carrying $1.2 million-worth of cigarettes in Victoria. Police caught him in the act, and after he was handed a jail sentence, his DNA was uploaded to the national DNA database.

This meant that, in 2020, police finally linked Fabriczy’s DNA to the milk bottle from the Palasics’ fridge.

Irma Palasics’ family, including her grandson John Mikita (third from right), attended court on Friday to watch the sentencing. Photo: Claire Sams.

In September 2023, Fabriczy met an undercover police officer and admitted he had gone to the Palasics’ house with another Hungarian called “Joe” that night.

Police then secretly obtained a DNA sample from Vekony that was linked to the water container. His DNA was also linked to the balaclava from the 1998 burglary.

Vekony denied the offences, saying he had never been in Canberra before his arrest. Fabriczy said while he did go to the Palasics’ home, he didn’t hurt anyone.

Justice Mossop said neither of the killers had shown any remorse.

Vekony has terminal cancer with a life expectancy of 12 months, so will almost certainly die in jail. He will be eligible for parole in December 2035, although he has lodged an appeal against his convictions.

Fabriczy will be eligible for parole in September 2034.

Speaking later on Friday afternoon, Irma’s grandson John Mikita said the sentence could not undo what happened to his grandparents, but his family believed it recognised the seriousness of the crimes and the devastating impact the two men had on his family.

“For 26 long years, we asked the one thing – that those responsible be found and be held accountable. Today, this has finally happened,” he said.

“There is no celebration. There is relief and gratitude, but also a deep sadness for everything our family has gone through and lost along the way.

“Today belongs to Irma and Gregor. After 26 years, they finally have justice.”

canberra.title: Police admit failures over response to alleged Belconnen Mall attack on young children
canberra.snippet: An ACT Policing practices review into the police response to an alleged assault of two young children at Belconnen Mall has found the inc...
canberra.content:
28 August 2026

An ACT Policing internal practices review has identified what went wrong when Triple Zero callers rang up about an alleged assault of young children at Belconnen Mall earlier this month. Photo: Westfield Belconnen Facebook, Michelle Kroll, Albert McKnight.

An ACT Policing practices review into the police response to an alleged assault of two young children at Belconnen Mall has found the incident didn’t receive the timely response it required.

It’s alleged that two children, aged 2 and 4, were in the shopping centre with their mother at about 1.30 pm on Friday, 14 August, when they were approached by a man unknown to them.

“The man knocked over both children before kicking one of them. One child was taken to hospital and received treatment for injuries sustained during the incident,” the police statement alleged.

The communications centre received two Triple Zero calls about the incident, but officers were not sent to the scene.

The accused, an 18-year-old, was caught by the mall’s security team but was released because the police did not attend.

Officers started investigating the incident on Sunday, 16 August, and arrested an 18-year-old man later that day.

The internal practices review was finalised on 22 August, and the media was alerted today (28 August).

It found the alleged incident and resulting Triple Zero calls were “not appropriately triaged or prioritised, and therefore did not receive the timely police response it warranted”.

“The review identified opportunities to improve training and operational call-taking processes within the Communications Centre, particularly in the assessment, escalation and prioritisation of incidents,” a police statement read.

“ACT Policing has commenced work to address the review findings and improve its response to urgent calls for assistance.

“ACT Policing remains committed to ensuring Canberrans can contact police in the right way at the right time, and that Triple Zero (000) remains available for emergencies.”

The delayed response resulted in a public apology.

“We did receive calls about the incident at the time, but police didn’t attend,” ACT Policing’s Deputy Chief Police Officer Richard Chin told the ABC on 17 August.

“Our response to the family at that time and after the incident wasn’t in line with our own expectations as ACT Policing, and certainly wasn’t in line with what the community would expect from us.

“We met with and apologised unreservedly to the family involved … We absolutely should have done better.”

The accused has been charged with one count of common assault and one count of assault occasioning actual bodily harm and was refused bail to reappear in court in September.

Given the police review of the response is an internal document, it will not be publicly released.

canberra.title: NSW Government’s little-known homelessness payments revealed as Wagga runs out of hotel rooms
canberra.snippet: Wagga Wagga ran out of hotel rooms earlier this week as the NSW Government continues to put homeless people into temporary accommodation ...
canberra.content:
28 August 2026

Start the conversation

The lack of affordable accommodation in Wagga has seen some people sleep in the vacant Murrumbidgee Mill building. Photo: Leigh Swansborough.

Wagga Wagga ran out of hotel rooms earlier this week as the NSW Government continues to put homeless people into temporary accommodation – while also quietly offering some homeless clients large payments to help them transition into permanent housing or move interstate.

Several housing advocates have told Region that Homes NSW has introduced a new product called “brokerage”, whereby eligible homeless applicants can receive up to $10,000 in assistance to help them move to another city, repair a vehicle or transition into housing.

Advocates who have attended Homes NSW offices to support clients have been told about the product, but it is not advertised and there is no public information about it on any website.

“What we understand is that if a client comes to Homes NSW and they need help getting to where they have promised housing – then Homes NSW will give them money to facilitate this need to get them there,” Wagga Ratepayers president Chris Roche said.

“That might be buying a car, fixing a caravan or paying for an airfare, and the payment can be as much as $10,000.

“But the problem is people don’t know about it, so they don’t ask about it.”

Region asked Homes NSW to explain the scheme and why it was not publicly advertised.

“Homes NSW and our Specialist Homelessness Services can provide brokerage assistance to eligible clients as part of an individual support plan,” a spokesperson said.

“Brokerage provides financial assistance to help people who are homeless in temporary accommodation to exit into alternative accommodation. It is tailored to a person’s circumstances and is not a standard payment or grant available through public application.”

At the same time, the department has refused to reveal how much it is spending on hotel and motel rooms in Wagga, or even how many homeless people it has placed in them.

The revelations come as Wagga’s hotel supply has been stretched to breaking point.

On Tuesday (August 25) there were effectively no hotel or motel rooms available in Wagga, leaving the NSW Government and Wagga City Council with nowhere obvious to put people being moved on from the Wilks Park homeless camp.

Region could only find one room available online, at a cost of $999 at the International Hotel.

Council rangers did not attend the park that day.

Region has previously reported that people living in tents, caravans and makeshift camps at Wilks Park have been threatened with $1000 fines if they refuse to leave.

Housing Minister Rose Jackson told a parliamentary hearing earlier this month that homeless people were being moved into hotels because there was no social housing available and nowhere else to put them.

Minister Rose Jackson was questioned on the Wagga housing crisis at a parliamentary hearing earlier this month. Photo: Supplied.

Mr Roche said there was a danger the strategy could hurt Wagga’s tourism industry, given the city already had a limited supply of accommodation.

“It’s concerning when there are nights where every single hotel is booked out. Where will people who visit Wagga stay?” he said.

However, the department insists its use of hotels is not significantly contributing to Wagga’s accommodation shortage.

It told Region it currently used six accredited hotel and motel providers in Wagga for temporary accommodation.

It said this represented a small proportion of the more than 200 accommodation providers operating across the city and that there was no evidence to suggest its use of emergency accommodation for the homeless was having a significant impact on broader accommodation availability.

But the department would not answer the more important questions about the scale and cost of the program.

Region asked how many homeless people Link2Home had placed in Wagga hotels and motels since 1 June.

Homes NSW did not provide a figure.

Region also asked for the average nightly cost to taxpayers and the highest rate paid since June.

Again, no figure was provided.

Homes NSW said it did not disclose the cost of individual accommodation arrangements because prices varied between providers and might be subject to commercial-in-confidence arrangements.

Region understands some private motel operators have been charging up to $500 a night for each homeless client.

Mr Roche said this was a poor use of taxpayers’ money, arguing hotels were unsuitable for people experiencing homelessness and that a serviced temporary camp with wraparound support would be cheaper and more effective.

Original Article published by Oliver Jacques on Region Riverina.

canberra.title: PM shuts down his Immigration Minister over refugee numbers
canberra.snippet: Anthony Albanese has pulled rank over Australia’s refugee intake, promising not to cut the numbers despite one of his Cabinet members sug...
canberra.content:
Prime Minister Anthony Albanese has promised no reduction in Australia’s refugee intake numbers, despite Immigration Minister Tony Burke suggesting otherwise. Photo: Thomas Lucraft.

Anthony Albanese has pulled rank over Australia’s refugee intake, promising not to cut the numbers despite one of his Cabinet members suggesting they would be.

The Prime Minister moved to quell reported speculation that Immigration Minister Tony Burke was slashing the annual refugee from 20,000 to 13,750.

“The refugee intake needs to be renewed in the coming budget as the 20,000 places were available for four years,” Mr Albanese told the ABC on Thursday (27 August).

“This intake number remains government policy and will be continued in future years, consistent with Australia’s humanitarian commitments and sits beside our strong border security measures.”

This contradicts the Australian Financial Review’s earlier reporting that Mr Burke had confirmed plans to reduce the humanitarian intake next financial year by 6250.

The Immigration Minister reportedly told the AFR the government’s decision to lift the refugee intake in 2023 was only meant to be temporary and funded for four years.

But an apparent Labor backbench revolt led to the PM overruling his Minister and committing to continue the funding for 20,000 a year.

The ALP National Conference in July reached unanimous agreement to keep the 20,000 per year while also aspiring to reach 27,000 in future years.

The Refugee Council of Australia indicated it had been told of the cuts before the backflip was announced.

Co-chief executive officer Paul Power said the Federal Government would be betraying “values held dear by Australian Labor Party members and supporters” if it went ahead with plans to cut the refugee program.

“When the Albanese government increased the Refugee and Humanitarian Program to 20,000 places in 2023, there was no hint that this was a short-term increase,” Mr Power said.

“The change was in line with the Labor Party’s long-term goal to increase the program to 27,000 places, an aspiration which has been in the ALP National Platform since 2012.

“It brought the program back to the level achieved by the Gillard government in 2012-13, reversing the cuts of the Liberal-National Coalition.”

The backdown has led to suggestions that Labor’s migration policy is becoming as muddled as One Nation’s, with its leader Pauline Hanson recently contradicting her newest MP David Farley on its overall migration numbers.

Mr Burke had planned to announce a significant overhaul to migration policy at the National Press Club recently, but he suddenly cancelled his appearance.

Deputy Opposition Leader Jane Hume said the government doesn’t appear to know its own migration position.

“Labor needs to announce their policy now because they’re in charge. They’re pulling the levers, but they are all over the place,” Senator Hume said.

“Tony Burke’s already had his speech cancelled. He’s already had the Prime Minister contradicting him publicly.

“Labor needs to make up their mind where they’re going to need to go.”

Greens senator David Shoebridge said the issue had put asylum seekers in “absolute tumult” for a day over the government’s intentions and sudden about-face.

“Minister Burke wouldn’t have presented those savage cuts unless he’d been through a process,” Senator Shoebridge said.

“And then it’s turned on its head by the Prime Minister in less than 24 hours.

“It’s the 24-hour news cycle, watching how people are reacting, a handful of MPs are reacting, the community response.

“That’s what produces this flip within 24 hours, an utter lack of principle.”

Labor insists there was no backflip, however, with Health Minister Mark Butler defending the bizarre antics during media interviews Friday morning.

“This is not a backflip, this is a restatement of a position,” he said.

“I think we should all take the word of the Prime Minister for the position of the government. We’ve had for many years a humanitarian intake number of 20,000. We only reaffirmed it at our national conference last month in Adelaide.

“I mean, yes, it has to go through the usual process of budget renewal, but there’s been no change for a number of years in the Australian Labor Party position on the humanitarian intake… I can say there was no position change by government.”

Opposition Leader Angus Taylor has left the door open to a future Coalition government reducing Australia’s annual refugee intake below the current 20,000.

“When we see what housing construction looks like we will announce the number and the visa classes will align with that,” Mr Taylor said.

“What is clear though is we are a very generous country, but charity starts at home and we have got to do the right thing by Australians first.”

australia.title: ‘So desperately loved’: ADF member among dozens of Australians missing in Nepal floods as families pray for safe return
australia.snippet: Relatives ‘really worried, but hopeful’ as they wait anxiously for news in the aftermath of the flash flooding disaster Follow our Austra...
australia.content:
The families of an Australian defence force member and two Sydney boys who went missing with their parents in Nepal remain hopeful they will be found safe.

Dozens of Australians are missing after devastating flooding on the Nepal-Tibet border. Nepal’s disaster management authority said on Friday that the total number of people missing had risen sharply to more than 1,900 swelled by 933 workers on hydropower projects on the Bhotekoshi and Trishuli rivers where a wall of water powered down on Wednesday morning. The number of people killed is at least 584.

One Australian woman contacted her family on Friday morning to tell them that she had survived the flood, the first of those reported missing to be confirmed safe.

Among the missing Australians is Karan Bhardwaj, a 40-year-old Brisbane-based member of the Royal Australian air force who was travelling in Nepal with Kailash Journeys.

“Karan is a dad to my beautiful seven-year-old nephew, as well as a brother, uncle and brother in law,” said his family member Jen, who did not want her surname published.

“He is so desperately loved by his family and right now we are desperately praying, hoping and believing that Karan is safe, alive and somehow making his way back to us.”

Shylaja Muralitharan, 42, her husband, Chandrasekaran Muralitharan, 47, and their two sons Ashwin, 14, and Aarush, 11, were taking part in a pilgrimage when the flood hit on Wednesday.

Shylaja’s younger sister, Vaishnavi, said that she had lost contact with the family shortly after breakfast on the morning of the flood.

The family of four planned to head towards an immigration checkpoint on the Tibet-Nepal border soon after, as part of the group of 15 Australians trekking with the Himalayan Glacier Adventures tour.

“Just like everyone else that’s part of that group, we’re really worried, but hopeful,” Vaishnavi said.

“Hopeful that they’re safe and just waiting to be rescued.

“It’s a very difficult time for our whole family … I just want to make people aware that they’re there, and we’re waiting, and we just want them to return.”

Vaishnavi, who asked that her surname not be published, confirmed the family were close with other members of the group who had also travelled from Sydney for the Hindu pilgrimage to Mount Kailash in Tibet.

The family had been training together for the long walk, she said.

“They had been planning for some time, and preparing, because it’s quite a trek.

“They were all working very hard together to make sure they could successfully complete it.

“We just didn’t expect anything like this.”

Vaishnavi said it was difficult to get clear information about what was being done to find those missing. She has spoken with Department of Foreign Affairs and Trade officials.

“We do want to know what efforts are being made … we’re not aware of what is actually happening there.”

Australian woman Sumi Adhikari was at an immigration office at the Gyirong Post crossing when the flood waters hit. She was travelling with an Isha Foundation pilgrimage to the region.

Her husband, Nava Pandey, has travelled to Nepal and is desperately seeking information about her whereabouts.

“She was in the same area when the flood happened,” said a flyer produced by Adhikari’s family, and published with their permission. “If anyone has seen her or has any information about her, please contact the family immediately.”

Bharat Mangwani, 42, was travelling with the Isha Foundation as part of a pilgrimage to Lake Manasarovar when his family lost contact with him on Wednesday morning.

He was last seen at Gyirong before the group was set to depart for Kathmandu and then Delhi, his close friend Kushagra Tiwari said.

Mangwani’s family, including his nine-year-old son and three-year-old daughter, have travelled to India with a family friend, while his wife has gone on to Kathmandu to look for any information.

“All of us are praying for him and hopefully he comes back to us soon,” Tiwari said.

Suhasini Kandimalla, a mother of two from Springfield, near Brisbane, has also been reported missing.

Her sister, Supreethini Kandimalla, said that she was doing the hike with another Springfield local.

While she was a New Zealand citizen, Suhasini had been approved for Australian citizenship, her sister said. She had planned to attend a citizenship ceremony for it to be granted soon after she returned.

“I don’t know if it was a religious calling for her to do it,” Supreethini told the Guardian.

“But she certainly loved the treks in New Zealand too, and would go on lots of long hikes.”

A Brisbane man, Narayan Panthi, is also missing in the region. According to Nepal police, he was travelling with Kathmandu Holiday but he has also been conducting charity work in the capital with an education fund, the NeNas Foundation.

Panthi’s cousin, Amrit Bhusal, said his family was devastated but “holding on to hope and praying for positive news”.

“We are still hoping,” Bhusal said. “We are still searching. We are still praying for Narayan to come home safely.”

Bhusal said Panthi was “helping disadvantaged children in Nepal reach their full potential through education”.

New South Wales couple Venkatraman Balakrishnan, 52, and his wife, Chitra Venkatraman, 46, were also among the 15 Australians travelling to Mount Kailash.

So too were Sreedharan and Lakshmi Iyer, and their adult sons Rishab, 23, and Rudhra, 20.

The brothers played cricket for West Pennant Hills Cherrybrook Cricket Club in Sydney’s north-west.

“WPHCCC is aware of the reports that two of our players, Rishab and Rudhra Iyer, along with their family members and other Australians, are unaccounted for in the ongoing floods in Nepal,” the club said in a statement.

“We continue to live in hope, and our thoughts are currently with them, their loved ones and all affected by this tragedy in Nepal.”

The University of Newcastle’s vice-chancellor, Alex Zelinsky, said Rishab and Rudhra were both medical students the at the university.

“We are thinking of them, their families, their fellow students and teaching staff, as well as the many people who have been impacted by this devastating event and we hope that both students can be located soon,” Zelinsky said in a statement.

Separate groups of Australians – 11 travelling with Trekkers Society and six with Kailash Journeys – are also unaccounted for. Both tour companies have been contacted for comment.

Several other Australians were travelling with other tour groups. It is understood the majority of missing Australians are from New South Wales, but there are also some from Victoria and Queensland.

The founder and chief executive of Himalayan Glacier Adventures, Sagar Pandey, said he had lost all contact with his tour group of 47 people, which included the 15 Australians.

Pandey told the Guardian on Thursday he had flown by helicopter over the Rasuwa area, where the tour was staying, since the flood and had little hope they survived.

“To be honest … you would think there was no human civilisation there at all.

“The flash flood swept away everything, everything. You couldn’t see any human creations.

“Still, I have a hope.”

The Isha Foundation confirmed that 11 Australians were among a group of 80 missing pilgrims who had been in an immigration building when the flood hit.

The foreign minister, Penny Wong, spoke to her Nepali counterpart, Shisir Khanal, on Friday evening to convey Australia’s deepest condolences following the devastating floods.

She outlined Australia’s humanitarian assistance package in which Australia was “rapidly mobilising consular and humanitarian support in response” to the flooding.

Wong said the government would send an initial team of three humanitarian response specialists “within the next 48 hours’” to help Australian staff already on the ground.

“The extraordinary scale of this disaster and the remoteness of the affected region mean immense challenges lie ahead for the response and recovery.”

australia.title: How Nepali diaspora is responding to flood disaster and how Australians can help in relief effort
australia.snippet: Nepali and Tibetan communities plan vigils and work to raise funds for recovery in ‘devastating’ time Get our breaking news email , free ...
australia.content:
Australia’s Nepali community plan to host vigils to remember the victims of the Nepal-Tibet flood disaster to coincide with a day of mourning, as the number of people killed continues to rise.

As Australia’s Nepali diaspora wait for the full scale of the disaster to become clear, community members are desperately waiting to hear from missing relatives and friends.

Nepali authorities said on Friday that the death toll had risen to 579, with the number missing rising sharply to more than 1,900, after massive flash floods and landslides tore through the Bhotekoshi and Trishuli river basins on Wednesday.

The foreign affairs minister, Penny Wong, on Friday morning confirmed the number of Australians missing in the floods had increased to 39 as she unveiled a $5m support package.

Wong told the ABC that Australians who wished to donate could do so via the Emergency Action Alliance website – run by a group of Australian charities and humanitarian organisations.

Nepali Australians gathered for candlelight prayers on Thursday night and held a minute’s silence for those lost to the floods.

Dr Tilak Pokhrel, president of the Australian Nepalese Multicultural Centre (ANMC), said community organisations in Victoria would host a vigil when the Nepali government announced an upcoming national day of mourning.

“Community members just want to say we are with you for those who are affected,” he said.

“We want to have an event where we all can gather and show our solidarity to support them.

“Let’s work together, let’s pray together, and let’s go through this pain together.”

Pokhrel said the centre would extend its opening hours for the next few days so faith leaders could provide support.

“People are waiting for the news. They are checking the news every hour,” he said.

Chudamani Sapkota, the general secretary of Non-Resident Nepali Association, said its New South Wales branch would host a candlelight vigil on Saturday evening in Sydney.

“This is devastating news for all the Nepalese diaspora,” he said.

Sapkota said the organisation was trying to support Nepali Australians seeking to locate their missing relatives.

“There’s no network, nothing at the moment,” he said. “This is a very tough time.”

Melbourne student Rakshya Pandey’s family home and two grocery shops in the Nuwakot district, hit by the flash flooding, have been destroyed. Her father, who was injured after being struck by an object in the flooding, is receiving treatment in a Kathmandu hospital.

“Whenever I see the detail of the people missing or the flood or everything, it’s just so scary, and I’m scared … I can’t do anything. I feel so helpless,” she said.

Pandey fears there will be future flooding in Nepal.

Ashok Bahadur Dhungel, who lives in Canberra, has been trying to reach his nephew who works for the Upper Trishuli hydropower plant, which sat on one of the Nepali rivers that flooded. He said his nephew has not been online for two days.

“We hope he is still alive,” he said.

Dhungel heard through friends that his mother, who lives in the Nuwakot district, had survived. But he has been unable to speak to her due to power outages.

“She is everything to me,” he said.

Tenzin Khangsar, co-chair of the Australia Tibet Council, said the Tibetan community was “shocked and devastated” about the flooding. He said prayer events would be planned to commemorate the victims.

Diaspora community organisations are also crowdfunding for the Nepali government’s disaster relief fund.

Chiran Tiwari, president of the Nepalese Welfare Society based in Sydney, said the organisation had created a GoFundMe page to raise money for the Nepali prime minister’s natural disaster relief fund.

Tiwari said one of the welfare society’s executive member’s relatives was missing in Nepal, with the community rallying around to provide support to them.

“The situation is very sad for the community,” he said. “Everyone’s eyes is tearing so the situation is very difficult.”

On Thursday night, the ANMC hosted a candlelight multi-faith prayer night in Melbourne for people grieving the disaster.

australia.title: How is One Nation influencing Labor’s immigration policy? – Back to Back Barries podcast
australia.snippet: Tony Barry and Sean Kelly , sitting in for Barrie Cassidy, examine the politics of immigration and asylum after contradictory policy stat...
australia.content:
Tony Barry and Sean Kelly, sitting in for Barrie Cassidy, examine the politics of immigration and asylum after contradictory policy statements this week from Labor and One Nation. They discuss how much Labor is being led by One Nation and whether the government is doing enough to make the case for immigration.

They also cover the concessions made by the Albanese government to the states on GST and renewable energy for datacentres, as well as the bumpy economic road ahead for Labor, with new inflation numbers suggesting interest rates hikes in the future

australia.title: Three boys crawled into a skip bin one night and by morning one was dead. How did it happen?
australia.snippet: A coronial inquest is examining the death of Indigenous 13-year-old Budda Spencer, who had for years been on the radar of South Australia...
australia.content:
On a cold night five years ago, three boys crawled into an industrial skip bin, pulled cardboard over themselves to keep warm, and – though they planned to stay awake – fell asleep.

They woke as a rubbish truck hoisted the bin and poured its contents – including those three friends – into the storage section. One boy clambered out before the lid closed. Another stayed low. The third, whose family want him to be known as Budda Spencer, tried to escape but was injured in the fall, then crushed as the lid automatically closed. He died at the scene.

It was 11 May 2021 in Port Lincoln, in South Australia, about 650km from Adelaide. Budda had just turned 13.

A coronial inquest is now trying to work out what went wrong for the boy, who had been on the radar of the South Australian police, the SA Department for Child Protection (DCP), and a range of agencies and community organisations for years.

Port Lincoln, a small coastal town on Barngarla country known as the seafood capital of Australia, boasts a glittering marina packed with luxury yachts and fishing vessels.

In the 2021 census, 6.6% of the town’s population identified as Aboriginal or Torres Strait Islander – almost three times higher than the rest of South Australia. That census also recorded a median household income that was slightly below the rest of the state, but that figure doesn’t capture the discrepancy between millionaire tuna barons at one end, and extreme poverty at the other.

So far, the inquest before deputy state coroner Naomi Kereru has heard that Budda came from a home described as loving but disadvantaged. Some who knew him well described him as a mischievous storyteller who was kind and funny, others as a troubled boy with hearing and learning impairments, who was often roaming the streets at night.

In Adelaide this week, hearings focused on the DCP’s actions and why it was not considered a priority case.

Adolescent at risk

Budda’s mother, Deborah Betts, the inquest heard, was desperately worried about her sonbut could not keep him home and was struggling to cope.

In her opening statement, Rebecca Schell, the counsel assisting the coroner, said Betts had a “volatile relationship” with Budda Spencer’s father when they were living in Ceduna, and that there were several alleged domestic violence episodes. In 2019, the father went to prison and the family moved to Port Lincoln.

In March 2021, DCP assessed Budda as an adolescent at risk. He was skipping school, and out on the streets at night.

At one point he stayed at a mate’s place. SA police family violence intervention officer Madison Sellick told the inquest it was “a very active drug address”.

His home, she added, was a mess.

“I recall seeing many mattresses on the floor with little to no bedding … lots of dishes piled upon the floor and on the different surfaces throughout the property and other rubbish piled up in corners,” she said.

Sellick said she had several interactions with Budda and his family. In April, one month before her son’s death, Betts told her he would “just take off on her” and she “felt like there was nothing that she could do for him any more”.

Sellick said she didn’t think Budda had a good understanding of police cautions, his offending, or his bail conditions. Schell told the inquest he had a hearing impairment, and a severe language disorder, but refused to wear a “hearing hat” that would have helped.

Tony Perks, a senior youth worker and manager at the Port Lincoln based West Coast Youth and Community Support centre (WCYCS), described it differently, saying the house was messy not in “a hoarding or squalor style situation” but in “the nature of a busy household”.

Perks said he “had a lot of connection” with the “mischievous” preteen.

“He would love to drop past the office or our youth hub and come have a yarn or share a story with one of the youth workers,” he said.

“He loved to have a yarn, he loved to have a chat and he loved to stretch his stories.

“We spent many a times hearing about fishing adventures where I’m pretty sure he didn’t catch crocodiles and the like.”

He also had a caring, loving grandmother, Perks said.

‘Inadequate supervision’

By 2021, Budda was increasingly getting in trouble. He tried to hitchhike to Ceduna, about 400km away, to see his family – but didn’t get far.

In late April 2021, he was arrested for trespassing and spent about a week in the Adelaide Youth Training Centre, a detention facility. No application was made for bail, the inquest heard, because Budda said he did not want to go home.

Betts was becoming “increasingly worried about her son,” Schell said.

“He was spending time away from his family home and he would run away from family when they saw him,” Schell said.

“Deborah Betts thought she was losing control of her son.”

A meeting between police, Aboriginal family support services, WCYSS and the departments for youth justice and human services was held on 4 May to discuss his case, under the state’s vulnerable family and young person framework. DCP representatives did not attend.

Perks says it was “frustrating” that DCP didn’t always come to the vulnerable families meetings, where information was shared. The community services can’t access the child protection system to see what’s going on, he says.

The inquest heard the DCP was understaffed and overwhelmed. They were only able to deal with the most urgent cases, and had to triage and assess notifications quickly, preferably within an hour.

Because Budda was not considered to be in imminent danger, deemed as having “inadequate supervision” rather than being abused or neglected, his case was not escalated. Lower tier notifications have a 10-day timeframe for investigation.

Betts last saw her son on Friday 7 May. The family looked for him that weekend.

On Sunday 9 May, police found Budda Spencer with his two friends N and D, but he ran away. That night, he and his friends slept out at the Centenary Oval grandstand.

On 10 May the boys went to the house where D had been placed, under out-of-home care. Budda wasn’t allowed to be there, so they were moved on.

A local manager for Aboriginal Family Support Services, Angela Backman, saw them that day.

“It’s risky being out all night when we don’t know where [you are],” she told them.

“Come home, make sure that you’re warm. We’re worried about you, your family is worried about you.”

The boys told her they would make safe choices.

They didn’t want to go home. But they did not want the cops to catch them out overnight.

So they decided to get into an industrial bin in the car park of the local Repco autoparts store.

At 5.15am on 11 May, the truck arrived to empty the bin. At 5.50am, Budda Spencer was declared dead.

The inquest continues, with findings expected by the end of the year.

australia.title: Charles Perrottet becomes Icac’s main character amid claims of hidden payments and political hit jobs
australia.snippet: The brother of former premier questioned over what, if anything, was done in return for $2m from developer turned fugitive Jean Nassif Ge...
australia.content:
Finally, we are hearing from one of the central characters, Charles Perrottet, in a saga that has occupied the Independent Commission against Corruption (Icac) for nearly four years.

It began with the dismissal of the Hills Shire council and a late night 2022 speech in NSW parliament alleging secret payments from a developer. It pirouetted to a pressure campaign allegedly to remove the then NSW building commissioner, and ended with real world impacts: defective high-rise buildings and thousands of unhappy homebuyers, with the developer nowhere to be seen.

Charles Perrottet, brother of the former NSW premier, Dominic Perrottet, finally began giving evidence late Friday.

He told the commission that he had met the Toplace developer, Jean Nassif, now a fugitive in Lebanon, in December 2019 and had, over several years, provided him with advice on how to progress his developments.

Charles and Nassif bonded over their “frustrations” with David Elliott, the former member for Baulkham Hills, and a key figure in the rival centre-right faction of the Liberals, Charles told Icac.

“He was frustrated with a number of things. I would listen to him, I would appease him, because I wanted information from him,” Charles said.

Elliott had opposed some of Nassif’s developments in the Hills Shire area, earning the developer’s ire. Charles, for his part, was angry about Elliott’s attempts to unseat his brother Dominic and was looking for information on him.

Despite having a full-time job at BP as head of strategy, Charles was remunerated for his advice, though not directly.

“Jeremy [Greenwood, one of the Reformers] wanted to know if I wanted to share in their success,” Charles Perrottet said.

“I said, I have a full-time job. I didn’t want to be paid. I said, you can continue to pay Anita [Perrottet’s wife] and look after her.”

Icac is investigating whether Nassif paid $2m in an undeclared political donation to a group of Liberal-aligned conservative men known as the Reformers, including Greenwood and Christian Ellis, in the pursuit of certain political outcomes.

In the first weeks of its investigation it focused on how these allegedly illegal donations were allegedly used to fund this group and stack branches with highly conservative members, and ultimately shift the Liberal party to the right.

  • Sign up for a weekly email featuring our best reads

But this week the inquiry has focused on a potentially far more serious issue from a public policy perspective: what, if anything, was done, primarily by Charles Perrottet, for the $2m from Nassif?

People like Charles Perrottet are not registered lobbyists. They do not appear in ministerial diaries because meetings on “political matters” with ministers do not have to be disclosed.

They can engage casually with key ministerial staff because meetings with staff don’t need to be disclosed anywhere. Many of those working for ministers have their own ambitions within the party and would be flattered by the attention.

First the good news: Icac works, but slowly

The inquiry might have taken four years to get off the ground but now we are seeing why.

Icac is painstakingly testing allegations of hidden payments made to Liberal operatives allegedly for consulting, and outcomes that were either delivered or sought from the Perrottet government.

Icac has gone through phone records, text messages, WhatsApp messages, mobile phone tower information, bank records, computers, tax returns and flight records, to track the movements of the key players and the money flow.

They even obtained CCTV footage of the main persons of interest meeting up in a hotel.

More challenging is establishing whether there is any nexus between payments and political outcomes.

Former builder commissioner David Chandler gave evidence this week of a whisper campaign, which he believed was aimed at ministers and the media, to have him removed.

Chandler, a 40-year veteran of the construction industry, is not under investigation by Icac.

A former minister, Eleni Petinos, gave evidence that she believed she was “used” in that campaign. She also said she believed she was sacked precipitously by the premier and that she thought there was something else at play. Petinos is not under investigation by Icac.

We’ve also heard about Hills Shire Liberal councillors being disendorsed and replaced by a committee of the state executive of the Liberal party.

Charles Perrottet and other Reformers occupied key positions on the committee.

The old Hills council had been opposing a Toplace development at Cherrybrook.

And of course Elliott lost his seat in parliament.

Conflicts of interests

The Reformers and others involved, like Anita Perrottet, deny that these payments were nefarious and argue instead that they actually did real consulting or lobbying work.

Charles Perrottet’s wife, Anita Perrottet, was paid $313,500 from lobbying company Beckington for 18 months in 2021 and 2022 for Greyhounds NSW work and $347,000 in 2022 in “project consulting fees” in the space of three months, “for being a sounding board” for Greenwood and JPG Advisory on Catholic Cemeteries Trust.

“That’s $660,999, that’s an enormous amount of money?” said counsel assisting, Peggy Dwyer SC.

“I believe that is what I was worth. Jeremy believed I was a huge value-add,” Anita replied.

Anita Perrottet nominated three clients: Greyhounds NSW, while engaged by Beckington, and Catholic Cemeteries Trust and a vaping company, whose name she could not recall, for JPG Advisory,

“A sounding board on what?” Dwyer asked.

Anita said her advice was entirely oral and delivered during face-to-face meetings with Greenwood or using her husband’s phone.

But she “could not recall” a single detail of her advice. By the end of her two days in the witness box she had said the phrase more than 500 times.

Icac has been unable to uncover a single document relating to these clients other than invoices issued by Anita’s company, Macquarie Consulting. No research, emails, marketing strategies or even a text were uncovered.

This was 2022, the same time as the NSW premier Dominic Perrottet and his cabinet were debating whether to merge the Catholic-owned cemeteries with the state-owned cemeteries.

The Catholic Cemeteries Trust was vigorously resisting the merger.

The Catholic Cemeteries Trust was very successful. Despite the issue coming before cabinet several times during 2021 and 2022 and an independent report describing the situation as urgent, the Perrottet government declined to act.

Dominic Perrottet did not respond to requests for comment regarding disclosures of family ties to cabinet.

Do you know Jean Nassif?

At first Anita Perrottet denied that she knew Jean Nassif or that Toplace was a client.

But in true Icac style, the bomb was about to drop.

She was shown texts about a lunch at Nassif’s house. She said she didn’t remember her husband attending the lunch, but was shown photographs of her children playing at Nassif’s house and texts showing she suggested her husband pick up a bottle of wine to take.

Anita was shown a detailed email she allegedly sent to Antony Anisse at another Liberal-aligned lobbying firm, Premier National, regarding a Toplace development in Epsom Road, Rosebery,

The development was facing delays in getting its final occupancy certificate and the email purported to outline an eight-point plan to overcome the difficulties. Anita was unable to say even what some of the acronyms she had allegedly used meant.

Dwyer put to Anita that she was being put in “an impossible position” and that she was attempting to cover for her husband, who in fact, was working for Nassif. Anita denied she was lying.

“It was a transparent attempt to create a cover for a sham arrangement that had been established by Charles,” Dwyer said. “No,” said Anita.

‘You understand that there is an offence committed if you lie to Icac,”
Dwyer said. “Yes,” Anita said.

What did the premier know about his brother

When he appeared at Icac, former cabinet minister David Elliott described Dominic and Charles Perrottet’s relationship as “joined at the hip”.

Dominic Perrotet is not a person of interest.

Chandler gave evidence that Dominic Perrottet had begged him to stay on as commissioner, which was exactly the opposite of what Nassif wanted.

“I went up and had a cup of tea with the premier and he said: “David, you’ve heard the sentiment of the members and myself and we would like you to reconsider,” he told Icac this week.

On the other hand we saw texts that indicate Charles was intimately involved in securing the NSW premiership for his brother.

In October 2021, Dominic Perrottet became premier after the surprise resignation of Gladys Berejiklian.

In the Independent Commission Against Corruption on Friday we got a rare glimpse into the frantic manoeuvreing to secure him the leadership and the key people involved in the number wrangling.

One was Charles Perrottet, the NSW Liberal party right-faction power broker and younger of Dominic, Icac heard.

In text messages he and his wife, Anita, discussed his role: “Well, it’s definitely true that he couldn’t have done it without you!!” Anita texted.

“But hopefully, you can work together now and going forward to both achieve your goals. Does he feel bad about Kean?”

Charles replied: “Yep, I told him what he needs to do there.”

Matt Kean had had an agreement with Dominic to become his deputy leader, in return for delivering moderate votes, but ultimately appointed Stuart Ayres.

They also discussed pushing council matters with the premier, and also getting rid of David Elliott.

“That’s a call for tomorrow. I told him to turn his phone off and savour the moment with Helen, as tomorrow and Tuesday is going to be crucial in showing unity, we execute the prick as soon as party room is over.”

world.title: Egyptian queen’s 673-diamond necklace stolen in Vienna smash-and-grab raid
world.snippet: Police hunt two suspects after historic 200-carat piece is snatched from Austrian museum during opening hours Austrian police are hunting...
world.content:
Austrian police are hunting two men alleged to have stolen a 200-carat platinum necklace encrusted with 673 diamonds that was on loan to a museum in Vienna and once belonged to Egyptian royalty.

Authorities in the capital released pictures of the suspects captured by security cameras during the heist at the Museum of Applied Arts (MAK), amid a rash of spectacular smash-and-grab thefts from European cultural institutions.

The unmasked men bought tickets to the exhibition before shattering a glass display case with a hammer during opening hours on Thursday afternoon and making off with the diamond necklace.

In an appeal for information from the public, police said: “The perpetrators fled with the jewellery in an unknown direction.”

Officers fanned out through the city centre and deployed a police tracking dog to search for the suspects. The Kronen newspaper said investigators believed the men were probably carrying out a “contract job” on behalf of a criminal gang.

MAK said the piece had been snatched from a jewellery exhibition that had been on display since June, featuring more than 300 works by the French designers Van Cleef & Arpels. No one was hurt, although there were several witnesses in the room at the time.

Documentation for the show said the necklace once belonged to Queen Consort Nazli of Egypt, who wore it at the 1939 wedding of her daughter Fawzia to Iran’s then crown prince, Mohammad Reza Pahlavi, who later became shah. The necklace was sold by Sotheby’s in New York in 2015 for $4.3m.

The MAK said the exhibition brought together about 200 “unique and rarely seen objects” from its own collection and pieces spanning the 120-year history of the Parisian jewellery house, from the Van Cleef & Arpels patrimonial collection.

A guided tour planned for Friday afternoon was listed as “cancelled” on the museum website and the exhibition, which was due to end on 27 September, was temporarily closed.

European museums have been hit by a string of high-profile heists since thieves broke into the Louvre museum in Paris during the day last October and escaped within minutes with crown jewels worth €88m.

In Spain on Thursday, thieves raided the Treasure of Villena, a collection of bronze age gold artefacts described as one of Europe’s most important prehistoric hoards.

This month, four of the most important works by the 15th-century Renaissance master Antonello da Messina were stolen during a national holiday from a museum in the Sicilian port city of Messina.

Two days earlier, Italian police said they had recovered three paintings by the French masters Paul Cézanne, Pierre-Auguste Renoir and Henri Matisse that were taken this year from a private museum near the northern city of Parma.

A report by Europol this month found that robberies at European museums are becoming increasingly violent, with thieves sometimes brandishing guns, assaulting staff and using sledgehammers, axes and even explosives to smash their way to targeted loot.

world.title: What could Meta’s US settlement mean around the world – and what now for other claims against firm?
world.snippet: Other governments could seek similar concessions, while separate legal action is pending in places ranging from Kenya to the Netherlands ...
world.content:
In October 2021, Abrham Meareg’s father, a professor of chemistry in Ethiopia’s northern town of Bahir Dar, was shot at close range and died outside his family home. This was in the middle of the country’s civil war.

For weeks, Facebook’s algorithm had actively promoted posts calling for the academic to be murdered, according to Meareg and Foxglove, a nonprofit organisation supporting Meareg’s lawsuit against the company in Kenya. These posts included photos of his father and his home address.

Meareg filed the lawsuit in 2022. He said he repeatedly asked Facebook to remove the posts and the company did nothing. Nearly four years later, the case has still not been heard. Foxglove said Meta, Facebook’s parent company, had “fought tooth and nail to avoid responsibility”.

Meareg said: “It’s a matter of numbers to them, a matter of statistics. It has been proven multiple times that our lives do not matter to them.”

On Wednesday, Meta settled a lawsuit brought by 29 US states who argued it had designed addictive products that hooked young people. The social media company agreed to pay $18bn and to change certain features of its platform in the US. California’s attorney general said it was a victory that would make “a world of difference for children and their families”.

But elsewhere in the world, in jurisdictions as far flung as Amsterdam and Nairobi, other claims have yet to be heard. Far bigger questions about the power of a single US technology company to shape politics and democracy everywhere on Earth are still to be answered.

For the US, the settlement is a victory. A jury has done what the US Congress could not – put controls on a powerful tech company. As a part of the settlement, Meta has said it will set time limits on children’s use of its platforms Facebook and Instagram and block night-time usage.

For Meta, the settlement is also a victory. Its share price rose in the hours after the deal was announced. Its CEO, Mark Zuckerberg, was not forced to testify. The sum it is to pay, while not meaningless, is far less than the states had sought – $200bn – or the amount Meta itself had suggested in a court filing it might have to pay, which was up to $1.4tn.

For the rest of the world, however, the picture is more mixed. The limits Meta will put on its US platform are, in large part, similar to limits the UK and Australia have already achieved through regulation. There are certain concessions Meta has now made that other governments could also demand: for example, while the UK plans to ban under-16s from social media platforms, it may wish to ask Meta to impose a default daily use limit of two hours for under-18s, which is what the company has agreed to in the US.

None of this meaningfully changes the equation for Meareg or what his case represents, which is that a massive US company, unaccountable to voters, unbound by transparency requirements, owns a worldwide digital commons that shapes reality for billions of people.

Whether courts and governments outside the US have the power to confront this fact is a far thornier question.

The central issue of Meareg’s case is Meta’s algorithm. This is the system that decides what content to show users of Facebook and Instagram. It sees you linger over a video about knitting sweaters, for example, and then decides you’ll like one about how to care for your spider plant.

It sees teenage girls watch diet content and shows them anorexia influencers. It sees young men search for bodybuilding content and shows them Andrew Tate. It is alleged to have amplified content that promoted the ethnic cleansing of the Rohingya in Myanmar. It contributed to the election victory of Donald Trump.

Meareg’s lawsuit rests on the claim that this algorithm promoted the posts that called for the death of his father, and that Facebook’s sparse moderation in east Africa did almost nothing to prevent this.

In the early days of the Meta trial in the US, it seemed plausible that states would push the social media firm to finally make some changes to this algorithm. Those changes had the potential to fundamentally alter how the company does business. Meta’s algorithm is intended to keep users scrolling, stuck on the platform, and then it shows them ads.

But that is not what appears to have happened. The terms of the settlement will slightly change what is shown to minors, in that they will not necessarily have personalised feeds. But it is hard to see this concession changing the equation in war zones or creaking democracies.

Arturo Béjar, an ex-Facebook employee and whistleblower, said the limitations were “the equivalent of saying: ‘Well, you can smoke as many cigarettes as you can in two hours a day.’ It doesn’t make the cigarettes any safer.”

It may be up to groups and individuals elsewhere in the world to try to push for these larger changes. It will be an uphill struggle.

In Kenya, the high court recently ruled that Meareg’s case against Meta could go ahead, after years of legal manoeuvring from the company to try to prevent it. It could now be heard in the next year.

Rosa Curling, Foxglove’s co-executive director, said: “Meta’s lawyers have spent years trying to prevent this important case being heard, thankfully without success. We hope that the news from the US is a sign that Mark Zuckerberg’s time is finally up.”

In the Netherlands, Repro Uncensored, a nonprofit organisation tracking digital censorship, hailed the US settlement as a “major victory”. Repro Uncensored has an ongoing legal case against Meta in the Netherlands for alleged discrimination against queer accounts, and plans further action in other European countries.

Martha Dimitratou, Repro Uncensored’s executive director, said: “The next stage of accountability must address not only addictive design but algorithms, discriminatory moderation and automated decision-making. These systems shape civic participation and democracy, and the companies controlling them must be held accountable globally.”

The European Commission released a charge sheet against Meta this summer saying the company’s features, including its infinite scroll, contributed to “unhealthy habits and compulsive use”.

That charge sheet is part of an investigation into Meta that the commission launched in 2024. It may lead to Europe pushing for larger changes from Meta, including to its personal algorithm.

It is unclear whether any of these groups or parties can succeed. Meta appears to fear US regulators and courts: after all, it caved after just four days of its US trial. It does not appear to be as intimidated by regulators elsewhere.

Earlier this year it managed to dodge a class-action lawsuit brought by a group of Rohingya refugees over its alleged role in contributing to a genocide in Myanmar. It will have the help of the Trump administration in opposing any EU regulation that could curb its reach in Europe.

Meta declined to respond to questions about either Meareg’s or Repro Uncensored’s cases. In an earlier response to whistleblower allegations that it fuelled violence in Ethiopia and Myanmar, it pushed back forcefully, saying it was “just not true” that the company put profits over safety. Regarding Meareg’s case, it has said it employs staff with local knowledge and expertise to “catch violating content” in Ethiopia.

Meareg said he believed that Meta expected him to give up. “They don’t know how I am determined for justice,” he said. “It is the thing you do for the person you love. If you love someone – and I loved my dad from my heart – then he needs justice. He needs a public apology. There has to be accountability.”

world.title: UK urged to help free British-Egyptian ‘arrested in Cairo over sister’s activism’
world.snippet: Lawyers claim Eman el-Shazly, from Birmingham, was detained in effort to silence her sister, a critic of Sisi regime The UK Foreign Offic...
world.content:
The UK Foreign Office has been asked to intervene to secure the release of a British-Egyptian woman who it is claimed has been arrested in Cairo because of her sister’s political activism.

Eman el-Shazly, a 45-year-old based in Birmingham, was arrested on 16 August while visiting Egypt. Her lawyers say she has been detained in an attempt to silence her sister Mona, a relentless and harsh critic of the Egyptian government on her UK-based YouTube channel.

Her two brothers have already spent three years in jail and, in May, were rearrested. They were previously held in pre-trial detention, facing charges of “promoting the ideas of a terrorist organisation on social media, as well as broadcasting false news harmful to state security”.

The UK Foreign Office has confirmed to the husband of Eman that she is being held in the Ramadan rehabilitation centre and her case has been given the same file number as that of her two brothers, Hassan and Eid.

The government of President Abdel Fatah al-Sisi has faced allegations that it frequently arrests relatives of political critics to put indirect pressure on the dissidents to end their overseas criticism of his rule or of state corruption. Much of Mona’s activism focuses on alleged cases of corruption inside the security services or public utilities, a highly sensitive subject in Egypt.

Arfan Rashid, the lawyer acting for Eman’s husband with whom she has four children, says that unlike Mona his wife has never been involved in politics, and had gone to Cairo two months ago to look after her ill mother after the arrest of her two brothers.

“There is ample evidence that Eman has been arrested to silence Mona,” Rashid said. He added that Eman had told the security officials she was no longer in contact with her sister, and that many family members had repeatedly asked her to stop her political activism in the UK, but to no effect.

Mona confirmed to the Guardian that she had been asked to halt her activism by other family members, including to take down her YouTube videos.

But she added: “I have done nothing wrong nor broken any law … I am a very strong woman, but it is very traumatic for me since 11 or 12 children are without their parents. It is a horrible situation, but the Egyptian government will not stop if I appear weak. The government is close to collapsing.”

Rashid said the UK government had recognised the practice of “punishment by proxy” in Egypt in its country profile policy and information note published in March 2026. Human Rights Watch and the House of Commons library warned in 2021 of an escalating pattern in which Egyptian family members of critics living abroad were being targeted.

Mona runs a YouTube channel in the UK that has 130,000 subscribers. She is also active on X, making specific and controversial claims about government officials.

The UK’s Foreign Office representation in Cairo has asked for access to see Eman but has not yet received a positive reply.

Eman’s husband, Zeesharn Moustapha, has said Egyptian police and security officers attended the family home where she was staying a few days before the arrest, and demanded that Eman tell Mona to stop publishing material against the Egyptian government.

On X, Mona has claimed as many as five members of her family have been detained or harassed by the Egyptian authorities. She wrote: “Kinship is something beyond my family’s will, and I invite them to disown me to save themselves from this despicable, illegitimate dictator. I am the one opposing Sisi, not five individuals from my family. This is a crime against humanity that does not lapse with time.” She has lived in the UK for 18 years.

Eman became a British citizen through marriage. Her lawyer has asked whether Alistair Burt, the UK’s new envoy on complex consular cases, should be asked to intervene by the Foreign Office. Burt was appointed a month ago and has been tasked with working to secure the release of British citizens held abroad.

Burt has already met Gurpreet Singh Johal, the brother of Jagtar Singh Johal, who has been detained by the Indian authorities for nearly nine years without a conviction.

The Foreign Office has been approached for comment.

world.title: South African police arrest two Thai men for allegedly smuggling parrot eggs
world.snippet: Bird eggs intercepted in homemade incubators at Johannesburg airport as officials try to halt wildlife trafficking South African police h...
world.content:
South African police have arrested two Thai nationals in separate incidents for allegedly attempting to smuggle endangered parrot eggs out of the country as authorities try to stem the tide of wildlife trafficking.

A 50-year-old Thai national was arrested at OR Tambo international airport in Johannesburg on 20 August, carrying 50 bird eggs in a homemade incubator in a hand-luggage bag, South Africa’s environment ministry said in a statement.

The ministry said preliminary investigations indicated that the eggs were from parrot species listed under the Convention on International Trade in Endangered Species of Wild Fauna and Flora (Cites), which regulates international trade in wild animals and plants to ensure species do not become extinct. It did not specify which species.

Another Thai national, a 23-year-old, was arrested at the same airport on 16 July, allegedly trying to smuggle 418 parrot eggs in two homemade incubator bags. Thailand’s embassy in South Africa did not immediately respond to a request for comment.

South Africa is battling wildlife smuggling on several fronts, from poached rhino horns and the bones of illegally farmed tigers to abalone shellfish and succulent plants.

The environment ministry said: “The illegal collection and trafficking of parrot eggs pose a serious threat to wild bird populations and animal welfare. Eggs are often concealed in improvised incubation devices and transported under conditions that significantly compromise their viability and endanger the welfare of developing embryos and hatchlings.”

Staff at the National Zoological Garden in Pretoria are incubating the seized eggs, the ministry said. “Several of the rescued eggs have successfully hatched and the chicks are receiving intensive veterinary and husbandry care to maximise their chances of survival,” the statement added.

The ministry said the arrests were carried out after a “joint intelligence-driven operation” led by its Environmental Management Inspectorate, known as the “Green Scorpions”, and police intelligence, border and endangered species units.

South Africa punishes the illegal export of Cites-listed species with a fine of 10m rand (£460,000), up to 10 years in prison or both.

world.title: Mpox is back – and in new countries. How can this outbreak be contained?
world.snippet: The public health emergencies in 2022 and 2024 saw the virus reported in 145 countries, but in the new cases children appear particularly...
world.content:
A fresh outbreak of mpox in Guinea Bissau – the country’s first – means the virus formerly known as monkey pox is back in the headlines. So what has changed?

Since 2022, there have been almost 190,000 lab-confirmed cases of mpox reported worldwide in 145 countries. Before then, outbreaks of mpox tended to be relatively small and in a handful of African countries, where the viral infection was known to be endemic.

What is mpox?

Mpox is an infectious disease that typically starts with flu-like symptoms, including fever, chills and aching muscles. These are followed by a distinctive rash, beginning as raised spots that turn into blisters filled with fluid before forming scabs.

It used to be called monkeypox, because the virus was first discovered in captive monkeys in 1958. But during an international outbreak in 2022, there were concerns that the name was fuelling racist and stigmatising language on and offline, prompting the World Health Organization (WHO) to recommend changing it to mpox.

It is endemic to many parts of Africa, with outbreaks historically starting when people ate meat from infected wild animals. But in recent years it has spread beyond the usual areas, with sustained chains of human-to-human transmission. The Atlanta-based Centers for Disease Control and Prevention said this month that mpox was on course to become endemic in the US.

Why is it spreading to new countries?

There are, broadly, two types of mpox, known as “clades”. Clade I was once called the “Congo Basin clade” and clade II the “West African clade”.

The latter sparked a major global outbreak in 2022 when it appeared to undergo some changes that allowed it to spread more efficiently from person to person. It is passed on via close contact – in that outbreak, mostly by sexual contact, with men who have sex with men at the highest risk.

In June 2024, researchers raised the alarm about a new variant of clade I in the Democratic Republic of the Congo (DRC), which also appeared to be spreading more easily between people. That grew into another major international outbreak, which was declared a public health emergency of international concern by the WHO on 14 August 2024.

“Emergence of mpox in more countries in west Africa is to be expected,” said Prof Michael Marks, of the London School of Hygiene & Tropical Medicine and University College London hospital. “Mpox outbreaks have now been declared in a number of countries in the region, including Guinea and Sierra Leone within the last 12 months.

“Mpox spreads by close physical contact. This makes it suitable to spread in a variety of different contexts, such as in close sexual networks, as was seen during the 2022 global pandemic, or areas where many people are living closely together such as settings with refugees and internally displaced people, as was seen in the DRC outbreak over the last few years,” Marks said.

What happened to those two big outbreaks?

The 2022 outbreak was declared a public health emergency in July that year. After contact-tracing and mass vaccination programmes, the status was lifted in May 2023. There had been about 90,000 infections.

The 2024 outbreak had its international public health emergency status lifted in September 2025, not because the disease had disappeared but because numbers of cases and deaths were declining and officials felt the situation had become better controlled.

If genetic testing reveales a new variant, or surveillance suggested an outbreak was spreading particularly fast, making people particularly sick or proving more deadly, global health authorities would be likely to step in again.

How worrying is the new outbreak?

Cases had not been reported in Guinea Bissau before this outbreak. Unicef said it was concerned that of 46 suspected cases, 23 were children aged under 15 and most of those were aged under four.

“The concern about children is that they are at the highest risk of severe disease and death from mpox,” said Dr Aula Abbara, a senior lecturer at Imperial College London and adviser to Médecins Sans Frontières UK. “Young children can become much sicker than healthy adults.” 

However, she cautioned that the apparent over-representation of children in the outbreak data should be interpreted carefully. She said: “There may also be some bias in the data. Families are often more likely to seek healthcare for a sick child than for an adult, particularly in a resource-constrained setting with a fragile health system, such as Guinea-Bissau.”  

Marks added: “Children have close physical contact with their parents and with each other, and in settings such as Guinea-Bissau are often living in cramped conditions, which make close physical contact and transmission more likely.”

Confirmed cases do not appear linked to each other, which suggests the virus is circulating more widely in the community and there are unidentified cases.

Are there vaccines and treatments?

The WHO recommends two vaccines, which can be given to people at high risk or offered to people who have been in contact with a known case to prevent further spread. The question is where they are available.

Marks said: “The major challenge remains that supplies of vaccines are best in high-income countries but worst in low-income settings, where the need and conditions for mpox transmission are highest.”

A new global stockpile is due to be launched within weeks, which should mean vaccines can be deployed more rapidly to quell outbreaks. Officials also hope it will allow manufacturers to plan ahead and produce more of the jabs by providing a clear, concrete demand.

An antiviral called tecovirimat did not appear any better than a placebo when tested on patients with mpox clade I in the DRC, although the question of whether it might help some immunocompromised patients – such as those living with HIV – remains open. That trial did show, however, that giving patients good, supportive care dramatically improved their chances of survival.

While vaccines remained an important tool for outbreak control, basic supportive care could be lifesaving, Abbara said. She added that strengthening surveillance, testing, contact tracing and broader public health measures would be critical to understanding and containing the outbreak.

“Vaccines are important, but outbreaks are not controlled by vaccines alone,” she said. “Early detection, contact tracing, supportive care and strong public health surveillance remain absolutely essential.”
